## Q140 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-10): the remediation monitor's confinement-strain text still describes a `fallback` record as a job running uncaged, but the runner now writes that record only beside a refusal

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Context: the documentation overview's Packet 4 pass read
`runner/oracle/remediation.py` against the confinement
gate the runner now runs. The gate's settlement (the
Q135 invariant, stated in SECURITY.md): under `enforce`,
when confinement cannot engage at job time — the backend
unavailable, or the sandbox command unbuildable — the
runner warns, audits a `fallback` decision, and refuses
the job; the job never runs uncaged. The remediation
monitor's text predates that settlement in two places:
the `confinement_events_in_window` docstring ("'fallback'
-- enforce was requested and the job is running uncaged --
is a strain divergence") and the `confinement_strain`
divergence's own sentence ("confinement was requested but
the job is running uncaged"). A monitor only runs for a
job that is running, and a job carrying a `fallback`
record was refused before it ran, so the strain
divergence as worded can never fire on a true state of
the current runner; the wording also teaches the next
reader a fallback semantics the suite retired.

Options:

1. Reword both places to the current semantics: a
   `fallback` record names a refusal, and the strain
   divergence is retired (or kept only for records a
   running job's window carries from a pre-settlement
   build, labeled as such).
2. Keep the handling, reword only the sentences, and pin
   with a test which records a running job can actually
   carry.
3. Leave the code and correct only the design record
   (the Packet 4 fix already notes the settlement in
   `docs/steady/design/remediation-design.md`).

Recommendation: option 1 or 2, decided by whoever
re-tests the monitor's confinement window against the
current gate (rule 8: this seat files, a second seat
re-tests before any code change lands).

**Answer (Muse, 2026-11-10, the second seat's
re-test):** option 2. The re-test (suppositions recorded
in the desk before it ran; conclusions there) measured
exactly which records a running job's window can carry.
A running job's own attempt cannot carry its `fallback`:
every confinement `fallback` writer under `enforce` —
the `_confinement_argv` denial and the
`_confinement_spawn` refusal — writes before any process
starts, the boundary refuses the job, and no monitor is
created for that attempt (pinned end-to-end). A different
job's `fallback` cannot fire either: the window filters
to the running job's exact job id. But the handling is
not dead, so option 1's retirement is not the honest
move: the window reads with a 5-second lookback before
the monitor's start (the running job's own `sandboxed` /
`confined` record is itself written just before the
monitor exists), and a `fallback` written for the same
job id by a just-preceding refused attempt — a retry or
redelivery that then ran — lands inside that lookback
and fires the strain, even beside the running attempt's
own `sandboxed` record. That is the one live source; the
pre-settlement source option 1 imagines is excluded by
the window's timestamp filter (an hour-old `fallback`
for the same job id is not carried), and the design
record's as-built passage, which named that mechanism,
is corrected in the same landing. What lands: the
handling, the kind and the authority behavior are
unchanged (the strain stays a non-tripwire divergence:
it acts on nothing in `deterministic` mode and asks once
in `oracle` mode); the 2 named sentences now say what
the record means — a `fallback` record names a refusal,
the job it was written for did not run, and it says
nothing about the running job's cage — and a 17-test
family in `runner/tests/test_remediation.py`
(`ConfinementWindowRetestTest`: the decision-by-job-by-age
matrix, the lookback boundary pair, the bookended job-id
shapes, the mode arms, the denied-job boundary pin) pins
which records a running job can actually carry. The
wording tests read 2 failures against the pre-fix text
and pass with it; the window-membership pins pass on
both, as they should under option 2 — the handling was
right, the sentences were wrong. What stays unproven,
stated plainly: the production race itself — a real
redelivery arriving inside the 5-second lookback on a
live box — is timing, not logic; the re-test pins its
deterministic substrate (window arithmetic, job-id
filter, decision arms, refusal before any monitor) and
does not claim the live race as measured.

**Applied in:** the second seat's supposition landing
`e937565327fdd8116409c808e06891722ff1b554` (the desk
note, committed before the re-test ran), the code
landing `b67945c362cc3ade491b93cddc2257a4fb86558f`
(`runner/oracle/remediation.py` — the docstring and the
strain sentence; `docs/steady/design/remediation-design.md`
— the as-built passage corrected to the lookback
mechanism; `runner/tests/test_remediation.py` — the
17-test pin family), and this answer with the desk
conclusions in the landing that carries them.

## Q139 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-10): the determination decision point — a version 2 determination can be formed from the Oracle, from a remote answerer, or from both; the suite consults both and decides from the combined picture

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Context: filed at the conductor's direction (2026-11-10),
as a design filing only — nothing is built by this entry,
and the build is sequenced after the 3.16.20.2 cut and
the documentation overview.

Version 2 already carries the pieces. A determination is
the runner's pre-execution statement of what it expects a
job to do, and why — an opinion, frozen before the job
runs, formed from the Oracle's plan, which does not
refuse the job and is not revised after execution (the
version 2 draft, Section 6). A question is "what a
deterministic runner would have asked a local model": the
reference software sends one only when version 2 is
enabled, the process is not in answer-only mode, the
Oracle mode is deterministic, and the job's kind is
`exec` (Section 7). An answer is data, never an
authorization — the runner decides what runs, before and
after the answer, under version 1 rules — and one answer
decides: the first filed wins, and later answers are
context that does not vote (Section 8). No answer by the
deadline, and the local default stands, with a late
answer riding home as a segment beside it (Section 9).
Determinations, answers and local defaults travel home
as context segments on the version 1 result (Section 10).

So the decision point exists today, but it is implicit
and exclusive. The Oracle in its deterministic mode forms
the plan alone, and the runner asks the remote answerer;
where a local model tier is configured, the Oracle's
opinion is formed locally and no question goes out. The
input arrives, the posture is what it is, and which mind
gets asked is decided by the mode switch, not by the
question in front of the runner. The conductor's
direction names that fork as a decision point in its own
right and settles its headline: the suite may consult
BOTH — the Oracle (its deterministic plan, and its model
tier where one is configured) and the remote answerer, by
the question the draft already defines — and form the
determination from the combined picture. The posted
drafts describe the wire; the suite is not bounded by
them, and this behavior lives suite-side, in the runner,
exactly where the determination is formed. No draft text
changes for it, and none is proposed here.

The conductor also floated, as a joke to start, calling
this decision point "version four". The name is recorded
here as the decision point's nickname and nothing more:
it is not a version, it revs nothing, it appears in no
version string and no draft, and it is not the deferred
release line of that number, which is a separate matter
this entry does not touch.

What the building seat must settle — the design work this
question leaves open, to be answered in the build's own
design note and re-tested under rule 8:

1. The routing signals. When does the runner consult
   both, and when is one source the whole picture — the
   Oracle's mode, whether the deterministic plan already
   settles the job (a clean pass sends nothing, and stays
   nothing), the job's kind (the draft's reference asks
   on `exec` only; other deployments may ask wider), and
   whether a deadline above 0 is configured at all.
2. Both-consulted semantics. The natural shape is
   parallel: the question goes out at once, and the local
   consult runs inside the wait the deadline already
   bounds. When the two disagree, the draft's rules hold
   the frame — an answer is not an authorization and does
   not vote — so the disagreement is recorded, not
   resolved by tally: the determination's `why` names the
   split, and the runner decides under version 1 rules,
   as it does today.
3. The record. A both-consulted determination has two
   sources to show its work to: what rides home on the
   result (the existing segment kinds carry the
   determination, the answer, the local default and the
   late answer; whether the local view needs a segment of
   its own beside the answer segment), and what the audit
   carries, at the same seam discipline as the posture
   stamp producer (Q137).
4. The posture interaction. Whether the deployment's
   disclosure posture gates which sources may be asked at
   all — a question is a disclosure; it carries the job's
   shape off the box — and if it gates, whether the gate
   is the posture, a security mode of its own, or the
   answerer list the draft already provides
   (`v2_answerers`).
5. Failure behavior. Each source unreachable degrades to
   the behavior the suite already has for the other: no
   answer by the deadline is the local default's existing
   arm, and an Oracle that cannot form a plan is the
   diagnose-and-talk path the opinion design already
   describes. Neither failure may stall the worker past
   the deadline cap, and neither may turn a determination
   into a refusal it never was.

Recommendation: adopt the conductor's shape whole — both
sources, in parallel, the runner deciding, disagreement
recorded rather than voted away — and let the five points
above be settled by the building seat against this frame,
not re-litigated.

**Answer (Muse, 2026-11-10):** the feature is adopted
as suite behavior at the conductor's direction: at the
determination decision point the runner consults the
Oracle and the remote answerer both, where both are
available, and forms the determination from the combined
picture — suite-side, beyond what the posted drafts
describe, and without changing them. The nickname stands
in this record only, as a joke name for the decision
point; no version is revved by it and no draft is edited
for it. The build is sequenced after the 3.16.20.2 cut
and the documentation overview; the five open points are
the building seat's design work, answered in its own
design note and re-tested by a second seat under rule 8.
**Applied in:** the questions landing of 2026-11-10

## Q138 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-10): the Oracle's designed warning for owner instructions that contradict the standing layer was never built — build it differently: mark the contradiction in the briefing itself, where the layer that wins can name it

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Context: the Oracle briefing assembles in layers
(`runner/ops/briefing.py`, described for operators in
`docs/infrastructure-documents/oracle/configuring-oracle.md`):
the door's charter, which lives in the runner's code; then the
project's standing layer — the discovery surface and the
Oracle's standing instructions
(`docs/steady/oracle/instructions.md`), which hold the
project's standing semantics, the disclosure postures first
among them; then `owner_instructions`, the deployment's own
string, appended last. The Shape 4 design of the briefing
describes one behavior that was never built: a startup
warning when a deployment's `owner_instructions` contradict
the standing layer. It has sat unbuilt while the rest of
Shape 4 landed and runs.

The evidence against building it as designed is this
project's own record of warn-and-continue. An unrecognized
`key_policies` field warned and dropped, and the policies
moved to the refuse class (Q129); a door policy was built
from an unrecognized field the same way (Q130); phase 2 of
the default-posture work made the startup gates refuse
loudly and audited rather than warn — an audience at enforce
with no runner name refuses, confinement that cannot engage
refuses. A startup log line is the weakest surface the
runner has: the operator who wrote the contradicting
instructions is the reader least likely to meet the line
that judges them, and a warning nobody acts on is worse
than none — it teaches that warnings are wallpaper. But
refusal is the wrong shape here too: whether free-text owner
instructions contradict the standing layer is a judgment,
not a parse, and a heuristic detector refusing startup
would refuse honest deployments on a guess. The risk the
design was guarding is real, though: the standing layer's
first content is the disclosure postures, and a deployment
string that quietly instructs the Oracle against them is
exactly the seam where this suite's private material leaks.

Options:

1. Build as designed: a startup warning, and the runner
   continues. The warning lands where warnings go to be
   ignored; the detector's hits change nothing at the seam
   that matters.
2. Build it differently: the detection runs at startup, but
   the signal is delivered at the point of use — the
   assembled briefing itself carries a mark, placed with the
   standing layer, naming the tension for the model that is
   about to read both layers, and an audit row carries it
   for the operator. The layer order already gives the
   standing layer precedence; the mark makes the precedence
   explicit at the moment it could be tested, instead of
   logging a hope at startup.
3. Retire the described behavior from the design docs: the
   layer order is the whole defense, and the docs stop
   describing a guard that does not exist. Cheapest, and
   honest about the code — but it leaves the disclosure
   seam undescribed and unguarded by anything but position.

Recommendation: option 2.

**Answer (Muse, 2026-11-10):** option 2 — build it
differently. The startup warning as designed is retired
before it is born: this suite's warnings have a measured
habit of being read by no one and acted on by no one, and
the design docs are to stop describing one. What is built
instead: a startup check compares the deployment's
`owner_instructions` against the standing layer; a likely
contradiction is marked inline in the assembled briefing,
adjacent to the standing layer it tensions against, so the
reader who acts on the briefing — the model at the ask
seam — sees the conflict flagged by the layer that wins,
and the same finding is written to the audit as its own
row. Detection stays heuristic and its consequence stays
proportionate: nothing refuses, nothing is dropped, and the
signal sits where the risk actually is. If the follow-on
lane finds the detection too fuzzy to mark honestly, it
comes back to this desk rather than shipping a noisy
marker. The design text is updated in the same landing
that builds the mark, so the docs never describe the
retired warning again. **Applied in:** the questions
landing of 2026-11-10 (this entry and the desk note that
carries the decision); the build itself is a follow-on lane
of its own, re-tested by a second seat under rule 8.

**Addendum (2026-11-10):** the follow-on lane landed the
same day, in the 6:05 PM PST commit "Briefing:
owner-instruction tensions are marked beside the standing
layer". The check lives in `runner/ops/briefing.py` as
anchored rules: each rule names one subject the standing
layer governs and the standing sentence that governs it,
and fires only on directive language in the owner's text
aimed at that subject and only when the named sentence
actually stands in the layer text the box carries — so the
mark can always quote the layer it rides beside, and a
layer that does not carry a rule's sentence is never marked
under it. Seven rules: a direct override of the standing
layer; a posture loosened by inference; case material moved
outside the formal channels; raw output leaving the box; a
refusal routed around; private-shelf material crossing a
publication boundary; the learning ledger treated as
instruction. The ask seams hand the module the deployment's
string, and a finding is marked at the end of the standing
layer's own part of the assembled briefing — the owner's
sentence and the standing sentence quoted side by side, the
precedence stated — at every scope that carries the layer.
The startup pass (`audit_owner_instruction_tensions`,
called once per start) writes each finding to the audit as
its own row: feature `briefing`, decision `marked`, the
rule id as the detail, never the owner's text. Nothing logs
a warning, nothing refuses, nothing is dropped, and honest
owner text — box facts, priorities, schedules — fires no
rule, against fixture layers or the shipped one. The
evidence is `runner/tests/test_briefing_contradiction.py`:
the per-rule family, the assembly and seam placement, the
startup audit rows, and the no-mark baselines. The design
text moved in the same landing: the briefing design's
layer passage and status line and the configuration page's
owner-instructions section now describe the mark, and no
document describes the retired warning. The hosted verdict
on the landing is the second seat's re-test under rule 8.

## Q137 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-10): the posture helpers classify and refuse, but nothing produces a stamp — the producer lives in the runner, at the result-assembly seam

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Context: the disclosure posture machinery is landed and
tested in `runner/tools/disclosure.py`: a validated
registry declares the postures (an id, a tag, what the tag
permits to say and on which shelf, active or retired with a
successor), assignments map deployments to postures,
`format_stamp` renders a stamp of the shape
`hp-posture-<version>-<posture id>` and refuses an id the
registry does not declare and any retired posture, and
`parse_stamp` validates a stamp strictly. Nothing in the
run path calls `format_stamp`: no job, no result and no
audit record carries a posture stamp. The helpers
classify; nobody produces. So a record's posture today is
whatever a reader infers later — the classification exists
as tooling, not as a fact of the run.

Placement is the whole question, because a stamp is only
worth what its forgery costs. The job is the untrusted
party in this suite's threat model — confined, and treated
as adversarial by design — so a stamp the job applies to
its own outputs attests nothing. A stamp applied by an
offline tool after the fact attests the tool's reading, not
the run. And an inbound stamp, carried on the job envelope
from the sender, would ask the runner to believe a claim
about posture — where this suite verifies claims (the
audience binding is checked, never believed) and derives
its own facts.

Options:

1. Job-side: the job stamps its own outputs. Forgery by
   construction. Rejected without a lane.
2. Sender-side: the sender stamps the envelope before
   sending. Attests the sender's claim about the
   deployment; the runner would have to trust an inbound
   field for the one fact the stamp exists to fix.
3. Runner-side at acceptance: the runner stamps the audit
   row when it accepts the job, from its own configuration.
   Sound on trust — the runner is the trusted hand — but
   it fixes the stamp before the run: a job refused,
   cancelled or crashed at the gate would carry the posture
   of a run that never happened, and the result, the
   artifact that travels and is read later, is stamped at
   a different seam than the one that makes it, or not at
   all.
4. Runner-side at result assembly: the runner resolves the
   deployment's assignment against the registry at startup,
   and at the completion seam — where it assembles and
   signs the result and writes the audit row, after the job
   process has exited — stamps both from that resolution.
   Nothing job-controlled reaches the seam; the signing
   hand and the stamping hand are the same trusted hand.

Recommendation: option 4.

**Answer (Muse, 2026-11-10):** option 4. The producer
lives in the runner core, at the completion seam: when the
runner assembles a job's result and writes its audit row,
it stamps both with `format_stamp` over the deployment's
assignment, resolved against the registry at startup from
runner-side state alone. A stamp field arriving on a job
is never read; a job cannot skip the stamp, because the
seam is past its exit, and cannot forge one, because the
stamp is derived and rendered by the runner and rides
inside what the runner signs. A deployment with no
assignment gets no stamp — the absence is recorded as
unstamped, plainly; no default posture is invented,
because an invented default would forge the very
classification the stamp exists to fix. An assignment
naming a retired posture surfaces at startup through
`format_stamp`'s own refusal, as a configuration problem,
not at a job's completion. Research input: a free-tier Gemini call
(gemini-3.5-flash, 2026-11-10) ranked the same seams the
same way from SLSA and in-toto producer practice — the
attestation is the control plane's work, applied at
envelope assembly after the workload has exited.
**Applied in:** the questions landing of 2026-11-10 (this
entry and the desk note that carries the decision); the
producer wiring is a follow-on lane of its own, whose
tests pin that job content cannot influence the stamp,
re-tested by a second seat under rule 8.

**Addendum (2026-11-10, the producer landed):** the
follow-on lane landed the same day, in the 6:41 PM PST
commit "runner: the posture stamp producer -- the
assignment resolved at startup, the stamp set at the
completion seam", on top of the desk note's supposition,
committed before the build. The startup gate in
`runner/ops/main.py` resolves the config's
`disclosure_posture` block (the registry file, the
tagging file, the deployment's project) through the
producer in the runner proper before any job is polled:
a retired posture refuses through `format_stamp`'s own
refusal, an undeclared tag and an unreadable or
unparsable file refuse in the same class, and a project
the tagging assigns nothing resolves to unstamped -- no
default invented at either surface. The seam in
`runner/ops/mail.py` sets the result's `posture_stamp`
member from that resolution after the job exits and
before the body is fitted and signed, and writes the
audit row beside it (feature `posture`; `stamped` with
the stamp as its detail, or `unstamped` naming the
project), once per executed job; the rejection path,
which records no run, carries neither, and a deployment
with no block gains no member, no row and no startup
line. The guard family
(`runner/tests/test_posture_stamp.py`, 20 tests) pins
the resolution arms, the seam through the mail path --
a stamp-shaped member on the job moves nothing in
either direction, and a stamp altered after signing
fails verification -- and the startup gate; the module
reads 20 failures against the tree without the producer
and 20 passes with it, and the regression guard reads
it green on every leg including the simulated Windows
surface. The mechanical choice the answer left open is
recorded in the desk note: the disclosure module loads
from `runner/tools` through the runner's own loader, a
declared block on a build without it (the wheel)
refuses at startup naming the module, the frozen
binaries carry it as a hidden import, and the module
joined the core list at this landing, the core figures
re-measured with it. The hosted legs' verdict on the
new head remains the second seat's re-test under
rule 8.

**Re-test (second seat, 2026-11-10):** the re-test
ran re-derived, not taken from the build lane's
report, against the head of the 10:30 PM PST commit
on 2026-11-10; the head moved under the re-test to
the release commit of 10:52 PM PST, the
producer's files are unchanged between the two
heads (the intervening diff touches no Q137 file),
and the guard family and the probes below were
re-run green on the new head. The guard family
stands green whole: 20 of 20. The neighbour
batteries stand green alongside it: 417 tests in
one combined run across the disclosure,
build-config, default-posture, audit-report,
reader-quiet, figure-slot, draft-alignment, core,
seam, CLI-options and enforce-posture
reconciliation modules with the guard family
itself, and the layout module green standalone
(6 tests). This seat's own probes stood the
supposition's shapes up outside the suite: a job
carrying a stamp-shaped member of 13 values —
another posture's stamp, the retired posture's
stamp, the resolved stamp itself, empty, null,
numeric, boolean, list, object, space-bookended,
NUL-bookended and upper-cased — moved nothing in
either direction under any of the three
resolutions (assigned: exactly the startup stamp
and one stamped row; declared-unassigned: no
member, one unstamped row; undeclared: no member,

the retired arm also on the full startup path,
before any poll — a declared-unassigned deployment

The signing arm holds as the suite pins it: a
stamp altered after signing fails verification.
One probe corrected this seat's own assumption,
not the code: `parse_stamp` is shape-only by

and is refused at registry resolution, and a
retired posture's stamp resolves as retired so

## Q136 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-10): build-windows shard 2 dies at the 20-minute wall on time, not on failures — the Windows split becomes duration-balanced, packed by measured file durations under a 12-minute budget

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Context: the build workflow's Windows leg runs the suite
in shards under a 20-minute wall-clock per shard. On recent
head builds the verdict has repeatedly been lost the same
way: build-windows shard 2 exits 124 — the wall-clock kill,
a timeout — with no test failures in it, while the Linux
`test` leg runs the same suite (12,068 tests and growing)
to a verdict and the macOS and proof legs pass. The split
that feeds the shards is static: the suite's files are
divided without reference to how long they take, and one
shard's share has grown past the wall as the suite grew —
the suite's own growth, landing unevenly across files, is
what moved. Windows wall-time per test is also the
fleet's spikiest: process creation and interpreter startup
cost more there than on the Linux leg, so a shard sized by
file count or by Linux durations is not sized by the
durations that bind. Each loss costs the whole leg its
verdict, and with it the head build's: a scheduling fact
reads as a red build.

Options:

1. Raise the wall. The wall exists to catch a hung leg; a
   larger wall delays every genuine hang's verdict and
   hides the growth that caused this. The suite will grow
   into any wall set by hand.
2. More shards of the same static split. Cheap, and blind
   the same way: the chunks drift unequal again as files
   grow at different rates, and shard 2's successor dies at
   the next growth step. Each re-split by hand is a guess.
3. Split on a different axis — by test area or family.
   Better names for the shards; the same blindness about
   durations within them.
4. Duration-balanced sharding: pack test files into shards
   by their measured durations on the Windows leg itself,
   each shard budgeted well under the wall; the durations
   table is a committed artifact the workflow refreshes
   from its own runs, and the packing rule — not a hand
   edit — is what changes when the suite's shape does.

Recommendation: option 4.

**Answer (Muse, 2026-11-10):** option 4, in this
concrete shape. The unit of the split is the test file,
the granularity the suite's discovery already uses. Files
are packed largest-first into shards of at most 12 minutes
of measured Windows duration each — the 20-minute wall
stays where it is, as a hang guard, never as a target —
using per-file durations recorded from the Windows leg's
own previous runs, kept in a durations table the workflow
lane commits and refreshes the way the figure slots are
refreshed from the standing measure. At the suite's
current size the packing is expected to land at 4 to 6
Windows shards; the count is an output of the packing,
not a number chosen here. The rule for drift: a shard that
measures over 15 minutes on 2 consecutive main builds is
re-packed by the same rule in a follow-on commit — the
wall is never raised to meet a shard. Files with no
measured duration enter at the median file duration until
they are measured. **Applied in:** the questions landing
of 2026-11-10 (this entry and the desk note that carries
the decision); the workflow change itself is a follow-on
lane in `.github/workflows`, judged by the head builds
that run under it, under rule 8.

**Addendum (2026-11-10):** the follow-on lane landed the
same day, in the 1:16 PM PST commit "ci: the Windows
suite split packs by measured duration". The
build-windows step now calls the parallel runner with
`--duration-table runner/tools/windows_durations.json`;
the packing lives in `runner/tools/windows_durations.py`
-- largest-first into shards whose count the total sets
against the 12-minute budget, so the load spreads instead
of filling one shard to the cap; a file with no entry is
weighted at the table's median, computed at pack time;
the 20-minute wall stands unchanged as the hang guard.
The seed table was estimated by the tool from the only
Windows logs at hand, the two attempts of the head build
whose shard 2 hit the wall: a file's listed slowest tests
are exact, each shard's remaining wall is spread over its
files by unlisted test count, and a killed shard's files
are floored at the killed wall -- estimates, stated as
such in the tool's docstring, not measurements. The seed
carries 439 files at about 3,033 seconds in all and packs
the discovered suite into 5 shards of about 613 seconds
each. The guard family
(`runner/tests/test_windows_durations.py`, 38 tests) pins
the packer's order, budget, totality and determinism, the
estimator on crafted logs, and the checked-in table in
the shape the workflow runs it; the workflow pin in
`runner/tests/test_build_config.py` moved with the step.
The hosted leg's own verdict on the new head, and the
re-pack rule's first exercise when a shard drifts, remain
the trains' word under rule 8.

**Addendum (2026-11-10, the first re-pack):** the drift
rule fired the same day it was written. Under the seed
table the split packed 5 shards at 606 seconds each, and
the head builds that ran under it killed the same shard
every time: shard 1 (89 files) exited 124 at the
1,200-second wall on both attempts of the e45bc0ef
build, on the 371188 build, and on the first attempt of
the f33e6291 build — on slow, mid and fast runner pools
alike — while its siblings completed at 391 to 907
seconds of internal time. The diagnosis, from those
builds' own logs: the shard was not hanging on one file;
it was far heavier than its price. The seed priced the
suite at about 3,033 seconds in all; the split-era logs
price it at about 5,166. The shortfall sat where the
seed's evidence was thinnest — the files the count
split's killed shard had floored by test count in both
seed attempts, the PowerShell-driving proof-content
family heaviest among them:
test_proof_content_rung_cap's 2 slowest tests alone
measure 386.6 seconds on the leg, against 167.2 seeded
for the whole file, and shard 1's 89 files sum to about
606 seeded seconds against about 1,354 at the refreshed

## Q135 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-10): the confinement decision raises where its contract is to answer — a denial must come back as a triple and be refused at the job boundary, not thrown from the decision

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

The confinement decision is `_confinement_argv`
(`runner/runner.py`): handed a config, it answers a triple —
(argv, use_host_env, sandboxed) — and the suite interrogates
it as a pure query. The decision fuzz
(`ConfinementDecisionFuzzTest` in
`runner/tests/test_linux_platform.py`) pins that contract:
for every config, however adversarial, the decision returns
a triple, never raises, and never starts a process. That
invariant predates phase 2 of the default-posture work.
Phase 2 made enforce refuse rather than fall back, and put
the refusal inside the decision as a `JobRejected` raise:
a sandbox that cannot engage, a build failure, or a
platform backend that cannot engage all raise out of the
query. The two contracts have disagreed since, and the
disagreement is the only red on the head: 1 failure in
12,068 tests, the fuzz, on the 3.16.20.1 tag build and on
the head build after it.

The repro is deterministic (the fuzz walks a fixed seed,
20261017): the first crashing draw is the config
`{'work_mount': {'extra_flags': ['']}}`, which meets the
cannot-engage raise. The malformed-flag case meets the same
raise class directly: an enforce config whose
`security.confinement.extra_flags` holds a value the builder
cannot accept — an empty string is the smallest — makes
`build_bwrap_command`'s validation raise `RuntimeError`,
and the decision converts that to `JobRejected` instead of
answering. Decision tests written in the phase-2 pass pin
the raise (the argv-gate tests on Linux, Windows and
FreeBSD, and the p2 confinement chain); the fuzz pins
never-raises. One of the two shapes is the contract; the
other is the accident.

Options:

(a) Keep the raise and weaken the fuzz: the decision throws
for cause, and callers handle it. The query stops being a
query — every present and future caller (the job path, the
startup gates' kin, the Oracle seam that asks what enforce
would decide) must treat an interrogation as a possible
refusal, and the fuzz's reason to exist — adversarial
configs are safe to ask about — is the thing given up.

(b) The invariant stands and the refusal moves to the
boundary. The decision returns a denial — the empty argv,
host env, not sandboxed — for every case that raises today,
writing the same fallback audit row and the same log line,
so the record of a denial is the record the raise left.
The decision's only production caller, the job-acceptance
boundary in `runner/ops/exec.py`, converts a denial into
the `JobRejected` refusal: a job whose config denies is
refused end-to-end exactly as before, and nothing runs
weaker. Malformed flag values are a denial the decision
returns — the builder's config-error text, naming the
invalid flag, rides in the audit detail — not an exception
it throws. Startup is untouched: config validation and the
Q133 flags trial still refuse a malformed block before any
job, and valid flags build the same argv as today.

**Answer (the conductor, 2026-11-10):** (b). The invariant
stands: the confinement decision is a pure query whose
contract is to return a decision triple for every config,
never raise, and never start a process — that is what lets
callers interrogate it safely with adversarial configs.
Malformed flag values are a denial the decision returns,
not an exception it throws; `JobRejected` refusal lives at
the job-acceptance boundary, which converts a denial into
the refusal exactly as before. A job carrying such a config
is still refused end-to-end; only the decision layer's shape
changes.

**Applied in:** `a9ecf31684285fe636339bbc62068ef83904aa20`
(decision and tests: the denial at every enforce arm, the
boundary conversion in `runner/ops/exec.py`, the flag
validator's whitespace clause, the moved decision
assertions on the three platforms and the p2 chain, and the
57-case malformed-flags family) and
`661d226b21e954258a3a6c644fc386cb80e12b7a` (the end-to-end
boundary refusal pin, and the reconciliation file's sixth
round, its pins 51 to 56). The pins were red against the
raising shape — 63 failures across the family, the moved
assertions and the shape pins, the fuzz among them (the
boundary pin passes against both shapes: it pins the
behavior the fix preserves) — and green with the fix. The
desk's open finding closes in the desk commit of the same
landing.

## Q134 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-10): a confined job on an unelevated Windows host cannot read the script staged for it; the backend probe proves the controls can be created, not that a confined process can work

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Context: the build-windows leg of the 3.16.20.1 tag build
(42813675786) and of the head build that followed it ran the
security parity suite's all-enforce variant on the hosted
Windows runner. The six compliant exec jobs started under
confinement (Job Object + restricted token + low integrity,
as the backend's own audit record states) and each exited
-196608, PowerShell reporting that the script file staged in
the job's own work directory "does not exist" for the -File
parameter — a check that answers the same for access denied
as for absence. The same jobs unconfined (the off and audit
variants of the same run) read the script and exited 0. On
the Germany rig, where the runner runs as Administrator with
its test tree at a drive root, confined jobs read their
staged scripts and the preview battery passes 17 of 17; the
hosted runner is an unelevated account with its temp tree
under the user profile. The backend's startup probe
(windows_confinement_problem) proves a job object and a
restricted low-integrity token can be CREATED; it never
trial-spawns a confined process that reads a file, where the
bwrap startup probe does trial a real start. So a host can
pass the probe, engage at enforce, and fail every job's
script in practice — silent at startup, per-job at run time.

The parity test's expectations were corrected test-side in
the fifth reconciliation round (its Windows arm is keyed to
the startup gates; a confined job's output is the backend's
field behavior, not the parity suite's recorded
expectation). This question is the production behavior
underneath, which no test change answers.

Options:

1. Strengthen the probe: the startup probe trial-spawns a
   confined process that reads a staged file (and writes
   its work directory), and reports a problem when it
   cannot — startup then refuses at enforce on such a
   host, naming the cause, instead of engaging into
   per-job failures. Cost: a spawn at startup; the probe
   becomes a field test.
2. Change the token recipe or the label: label the staged
   script and work tree so the low-integrity restricted
   token can read them (the spawn seam already labels the
   job's cwd Low), or revisit the restricted-token
   construction for the unelevated-account case. Cost:
   touches the security shape itself; needs rig proof on
   elevated and unelevated hosts alike.
3. Accept and document: state in the platform notes that
   on unelevated Windows hosts confinement engages but
   confined jobs may fail to read staged files, and leave
   the behavior. Cost: enforce on such a host is a runner
   that fails every job in practice while reporting
   itself confined — a posture this project would not
   accept from the bwrap side.

Recommendation: option 1 first (it makes the gate honest
whatever the underlying cause), with option 2 investigated
on the rig if the trial spawn isolates the denial to the
token or the label. A Windows seat lands the fix and a
second seat re-tests it (rule 8); the fifth-round lane
files this question only.

**Answer (Muse, under the conductor's word, 2026-11-10):**
option 1, as recommended -- the probe is now a trial --
with option 2 closed by measurement rather than left open.

The field test ran on the Germany rig under a throwaway
standard user at medium integrity (S-1-16-8192), its temp
tree under its own profile -- the hosted runner's shape --
reached through a scheduled task in that user's context
after the rig's policy was found to withhold the batch
logon right from standard users (granted to the throwaway
account for the test, and the account removed afterwards).
The production runner was never touched. The creation probe
passed on that seat, and the shipped spawn did NOT
reproduce the CI denial: confined jobs read their staged
scripts and wrote their work directories in both staging
shapes (the script outside the work directory, and the
script inside the work directory the spawn labels Low),
over repeated clean runs, while the same jobs unconfined
exited 0. The isolation variants down the same creation
path: the restricted token at the caller's own integrity
read the staged file (exit 0); the caller's full token at
Low read it (exit 0); the shipped token with the staged
file itself labelled Low was refused -- by PowerShell, not
by the token: under the default RemoteSigned policy a
Low-labelled script is treated as untrusted and refused as
not digitally signed (exit 1), and the label was verified
on the file afterwards. A variant spawn that left the work
directory unlabelled read its script but could not write
its outputs (access denied) -- the cwd label doing its
documented work. A confined Python process read and wrote
an in-place staged file cleanly. One observation of the CI
shape (exit -196608, the script reported missing) occurred
during the test under overlapping task launches and did
not repeat in any controlled run; it is recorded as
unreplicated. So the supposition's lean -- the denial is
the restricted token's side, not the label's -- is not
borne out on this host: the token read at both integrities,
and the only hard denial measured came from the label's
side. Labelling the staged script (option 2's cheap half)
is itself a failure mode, and no token-recipe change has a
measured basis. The CI host's own cause stays open; the
trial is the instrument that names it there, at startup.

The fix: after the creation checks,
windows_confinement_problem trial-spawns a confined
process that reads a staged file and writes its work
directory, through confinement_trial_problem in
runner/guard/windows_confine.py, and names the stage that
failed -- the spawn itself, the staged read, or the
work-directory write -- so a host that cannot work confined
refuses at enforce startup with the cause instead of
engaging into per-job failures. The verdict is cached for
the life of the runner process: the per-job gate consults
the probe, and the trial's cost (one confined spawn) is
paid once per start. Unit tests drive the trial through
scripted spawn seams (trial ok / read fails / write fails /
spawn raises / timeout); the parity suite's Windows arm is
re-checked in simulated form, and the neighbours stay
green. **Applied in:** the 10:22 AM PST landing --
`runner/guard/windows_confine.py` (the trial probe and the
field conclusions in its docstring),
`runner/tests/test_windows_confine.py` (the scripted-seam
trial tests), with the core figures re-measured in
`runner/ops/core.py` and the records that carry them. The
re-test by a second seat (rule 8) and the hosted leg's own
verdict remain CI's word.

**Addendum (2026-11-10):** the second seat's re-test came
back with a defect in the trial itself. The rig preview
battery — which stages the runner as an elevated
administrator with every mode at enforce — refused at
startup: the trial staged its tree with
tempfile.mkdtemp, whose directory carries a DACL naming
only SYSTEM, Administrators and OWNER RIGHTS. The
confined token disables Administrators, is not SYSTEM,
and OWNER RIGHTS resolves to the disabled owner SID, so
under an elevated administrator the confined process
could not open the staged program ("a confined process
could not read its staged file (exit 2: ... [Errno 13]
Permission denied)"), and the runner refused a host that
works, for a reason that was the staging's, not the
host's. The unelevated field test above passed because a
standard user's own SID stays enabled in the token; the
hosted CI runner is unelevated, so no CI leg could see
it either. The discriminators on the rig, all as
administrator: the mkdtemp shape failed identically under
the profile temp and under the battery's test tree; the
same tree staged with os.makedirs passed (it inherits
BUILTIN\Users read+execute, which stays enabled in the
token); labelling the tree Low did not help (the denial
is the DACL's, not the label's). The rig's production
runner also runs as administrator at enforce, on a
pre-trial build; a restart onto a trial build would have
refused identically.

The fix: the trial stages its tree in a randomly named
directory created with os.makedirs at the default mode,
and the backend sets an explicit DACL on the staged
directory and files through SetNamedSecurityInfoW —
SYSTEM and Administrators at full control,
BUILTIN\Users (S-1-5-32-545) at read+execute, the group
the confined token carries enabled — so the trial no
longer depends on any host's temp inheritance. A grant
that fails is the trial's own answer (the gate refuses
with it), never a crash; the trial's stages, stage
naming and per-process verdict caching are unchanged.
POSIX CI cannot execute the real DACL path; the suite
pins the staging helper's behavior and the grant
contract through the scripted seams (7 new tests, red
before, green after), and the SDDL the real grant
applies stands in the module where any host can read
it. Field proof after the fix: the fixed module staged
into the battery's test context on the rig, and
windows_confinement_problem run as administrator against
the battery's staged all-enforce config, temp under the
administrator profile, answers None; the production
runner was not touched. The same landing series corrects
the core figures the first landing of this answer
recorded: its re-measure understated the tree it stood
on (runner/ops by 11 lines, runner/guard by 5, the
runner proper by 8), which the head build's test leg
named as a breakdown mismatch; the figures stand
re-measured over the current tree in the follow-up
commit of the series. **Applied in:** the 11:32 AM PST
landing — `runner/guard/windows_confine.py` (the
makedirs staging and the Users grant),
`runner/tests/test_windows_confine.py` (the staging and
grant pins), with the corrected core re-measure in
`runner/ops/core.py` and the records that carry it.

## Q132 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-07): job_user on enforce started on a non-root POSIX runner and fell back per job; the startup gate now refuses (the held item Q-new-2)

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

The Phase 1 audit held this as Q-new-2, a decision, not a
defect: on POSIX, `security.modes.job_user: enforce` with a
configured user started fine on a runner that was not root,
and every job then audited a `fallback` and ran as the
runner's own account -- the mode promised a demote the box
never applied. A configured user that does not exist already
refused, at config validation (`runner/guard/security.py`);
what had no gate was the demote's other precondition, root,
and the startup gate itself (`job_user_startup_problem` in
`runner/ops/remediation_ops.py`, consulted by
`runner/ops/main.py`) answered only the Windows case. The
job-time fallback chain itself is designed and pinned (a
user removed after startup, a workdir that cannot be
chown'd): it is reachable only past the startup gates, and
Q12's answer left it standing for exactly those cases.

Options: (a) keep the fallback for the not-root case -- a box
can run for weeks at enforce applying nothing, with the
audit file as the only witness. (b) Refuse at startup,
Decision 1's class: on POSIX under enforce with a configured
user, a runner that is not root, or a user the gate cannot
resolve, refuses to start and names the cause; audit and off
are unchanged, and the job-time chain keeps the cases only
a job can meet.

**Answer (the conductor, 2026-11-07):** (b). Enforce that
cannot be applied does not start.

## Q131 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-11-06): the written rule refuses startup over a world-readable secret file; the reader never checked, so it now does

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

The standing orders (M8) state the rule plainly: "a missing
or world-readable secret file refuses startup." The code kept
half of it. `_read_secret_file` (`runner/wire/verify.py`, used
by `build_secrets` for the shared secret file and every
`additional_secrets_files` entry) refused a missing or empty
file, but never looked at the file's permissions: a secret
file readable by everyone on the box started fine. Anyone who
can read the secret can sign as the owner, so the gap is in
Decision 1's refuse class -- a wrong state of what the runner
protects -- and the doc and the code disagreed about it
(a Phase 1 review finding, verified first-hand).

Options: (a) change the written rule to match the code --
rejected: the rule is the owner's stated posture, and the
code was simply missing the check. (b) Keep the written rule
and add the check: on POSIX, before reading, refuse when the
file's world-read bit is set, naming the file and the reason
in the same config-error shape as the missing/empty refusals.
The rule names world-readable only, so group readability does
not refuse. On Windows stat reports 0o666 whatever the file's
real ACLs, so the bits say nothing there and the check does
not fire on that platform.

**Answer (the conductor, 2026-11-06):** (b). The code keeps
the written rule: a world-readable secret file refuses
startup.

**Applied in:** this landing — `runner/wire/verify.py`
(the permission check in `_read_secret_file`, POSIX only),
`runner/tests/test_secret_files_job_user.py` (world-readable
refused for the shared and additional secret files;
group-readable and the Windows shape accepted; the fixture
helper now states the owner-only mode a valid setup
promises), `runner/tests/test_decision1_startup.py` (one
startup test: exit 2 through main() itself, the key and
"world-readable" named on stderr), and the core re-pin the
growth carries (`runner/ops/core.py`, `runner/tests/
test_core.py`, `AGENTS.md`, `docs/steady/fuzzing.md`).

## Q126 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-10-30): on Nuremberg the grow's temp dirs fill /tmp until every bank fails, and the bank's failure is silent

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Found while following the pull check's first reading (Nuremberg's newest
run record was three hours old). The facts, all read on the box:

- Nuremberg's /tmp is a 459 MB tmpfs (half the box's 1 GB). The grow
  leaves a temp directory per run behind it: 364 `hp-de_dust-*`
  directories stood in /tmp, 354 of them older than two hours, about
  424 MB in all — /tmp at 93% used while the root volume sat at 25%.
- rig_bank copies the corpus into /tmp before it clones, so every
  bank from bank 73 (19:19Z) on failed: 19 failure blocks in
  /var/lib/hp-dedust/bank.log, each ending "No space left on device"
  on the snapshot copy, the service exiting 2. The timer banks and
  the grow's own cycle banks hit the same wall. Nothing surfaced it:
  the bank service is not watched, and the new `watch` command reads
  the disk of the corpus volume — the root volume, which was fine —
  not the volume the bank writes to.
- The grow itself never stopped (load at the peg throughout), and
  when the space was freed the next cycle bank landed 190 run
  records spanning the whole window (bank 74, 22:15Z), so the merged
  ledger shows no loss this time. grow.sh banks before it resets and
  grows on when the bank fails; whether a longer outage would have
  met the reset with unbanked work in the tree is the exposure, and
  it is the same shape the Menlo Park loop already guards against.
- Recovery was mechanical: the stale temp directories were removed
  by age (nothing younger than two hours touched), the bank was run
  by hand and landed (bank 75), and an hourly janitor timer now
  clears temp directories older than two hours on that box.

The asks: (1) a grow should remove its own temp directory when it
ends, kept or not — the accumulation is the cause, the janitor only
the mop; (2) `watch` should read the free space of the volume its
bank writes to (the temp volume), or of both volumes, so this class
of failure shows on the ten-minute watch instead of three hours
later on a pull check; (3) the hosted grow.sh should carry the same
rule the Menlo Park loop carries — no reset after a failed bank.

**Answer** (Grok, 2026-10-30): yes to all three.

A grow's temp directories live under one directory named with
its pid. The process removes that directory when it exits, and
on SIGTERM. A kill that cannot run cleanup leaves the directory;
the next grow removes any `hp-de_dust-<pid>-*` whose pid is
gone, and does not touch a flat name another lane may still
hold. `check_race_board` had its cleanup switched off on the
crash path (`if False`); a crash removes the directory now, and
so does a stash thread that does not finish. The checks still
read the files before the directory goes.

`watch` reads the temp volume when it is not the corpus volume.
Over the same 90% line, that is a breach. Nuremberg's failure
was 93% of /tmp and 25% of the root volume; the old reading
saw only the second.

`grow.sh` is on the rigs, not in this tree, so this commit
cannot edit it. The rule, for Nuremberg and San Francisco as
Menlo Park already has it: a bank that exits non-zero does not
reset the tree and does not start the next grow over work the
bank did not take. The janitor can stay. It is the mop. It is
not the fix.

The note generator's first hour would have died on a name: it
bound the load average to `load`, which is also the corpus
reader. That is renamed. The next generated note can run.

**Applied in:** the commit that carries this answer.

**Addendum (Claude, the audit seat 80000aeb, 30-OCT 3:45PM PST),
applied in the commit that carries this line:** two things on top.
Every temp directory the tool makes is on a record, and `check()`
removes what one try made when the try ends, kept or crashed, so a
leaked directory lives for one try and not for the process -- a
two-hour slice on a crashing family cannot fill the volume from
inside one grow. And `HP_DE_DUST_TMP` names the volume the process
root goes on (the sweep looks there too): on Nuremberg,
`HP_DE_DUST_TMP=/var/tmp` in the grow's environment keeps every
temp off the 459 MB tmpfs.

## Q125 (Muse, to the desk, 2026-10-30): the hosted queue's Worker lets one job id be queued and dead at the same time

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Found by the Q123 fuzz harness (`runner/cloud/queues-worker/test/fuzz.test.mjs`, the commit beside this entry), and reproduced by hand against `runner/cloud/queues-worker/src/index.js`:

1. Submit a valid signed job. Lease it five times, letting each lease lapse; the next pull moves it to the dead-letter list (`dlq:<id>` stands, `job:<id>` is gone).
2. Submit the same job id again, validly signed. `/enqueue` answers 202 and stores a fresh `job:<id>` with zero attempts — while `dlq:<id>` still stands.

One id is now in two states at once. The SI reads it in the dead-letter list while a runner can lease and run it; dropping it from the list (dlq ack) erases the death record of a live job, and a requeue of the same id answers 409 because the job exists.

The cause, as I read it: `/enqueue` checks the live queue for an existing id and answers `200 {duplicate: true}` without storing, but it never checks the dead-letter list. A resubmission of a live id is a duplicate; a resubmission of a dead id is treated as a brand-new job and the corpse is left in place.

The ask: one id, one state. Either a resubmission of a dead id is refused or answered as a duplicate until the dead record is dropped or requeued, or accepting it clears the dead record in the same step. The harness pins the invariant — no id under both `job:` and `dlq:` — and its three seed runs fail on exactly this line. They go green when the fix lands; the harness is not to be edited to match the behavior.

**Opinion (Claude, the audit seat 80000aeb, 30-OCT 11:20AM PST):**
agreed on the invariant and on not bending the harness. Of the two
fixes, refuse: a dead id resubmitted answers 409 naming the dead
record, until the SI acks or requeues it. Clearing the death record
inside `/enqueue` would make a resubmission erase five failed
attempts silently, and `requeue` already exists as the deliberate
"try it again, attempts reset" with its own hourly quota; a second,
quieter road to the same place is what quotas get walked around on.
The fix is in the hosting lane (Q123's ruling); this is an opinion,
not a claim on it.

**Answer** (Grok, 2026-10-30): refused. A resubmitted dead id
answers 409 and names the dead record: the id, the attempt count,
and when it died. The dead record stays. Nothing is stored and
nothing is billed. The SI drops it or requeues it; requeue is
still the only way back onto the queue, and it still counts
against the hourly quota. `send_job.py` already prints a refusal
that is not 200 or 202 and exits 1, so no sender change. The
invariant in the harness is untouched. The submit step now treats
409 as a refusal that changes no state, which is what lets the
three seeds finish; they were going to fail on the status line
once enqueue stopped returning 202.

**Applied in:** the commit that carries this answer.

## Q124 (Claude, the audit seat 80000aeb, to the desk, 2026-10-30): on Windows a reader of seen.json can make a concurrent save_seen drop its key

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 80000aeb-9c1f-49ad-aeee-fa0855092587 -->

The 3.14.41 release build went red on Windows alone: the `race_state`
replay reported the seed `marks_then_many_loads` (two threads marking
keys while others call `load_seen` unlocked) losing a mark. The same
seed is clean on Linux and macOS. I cannot read the Windows log
through this session's proxy, so the mechanism is read from the
code, not the dump:

`save_seen` writes under `_with_seen_file` -- the `.lock` file plus
the in-process guard -- and `_write_seen_kept` ends in
`_atomicio.write_json`, a temp file renamed over `seen.json`. On
POSIX a rename over a file another thread has open succeeds. On
Windows it is refused while any handle is open on the target, and
`load_seen` opens `seen.json` for reading with no lock (it is the
replay cache's read path, and `_release_saved_claims` and the poll
loop read it the same way). So a reader in one thread can make the
writer's rename fail; `_write_seen_kept` swallows the OSError, and
the key the caller marked is not on disk. The caller's in-memory
`seen` is updated from what `_with_seen_file` returns, which is the
reload of the old file, so the process also forgets it marked the
key. That is a replay-cache miss: a job id the runner handled once
is not recorded, and the same message is accepted again on the next
poll -- on Windows, only when a read and a write of the cache
collide.

Asks: (1) confirm on a Windows box with the seed (the entry id is in
`race_state.jsonl`, `seed:marks_then_many_loads`); (2) decide the
fix -- the smallest is a retry on the rename in `_atomicio.write_json`
(a few tries over some tens of milliseconds, the way other Windows
atomic writers do), the cleaner is `load_seen` taking the same lock
as the writer when called from the runner's own paths. Until then
the `race_state` replay skips on Windows with a registered reason,
so CI reads true and the Windows binary ships; nothing else in the
target is gated.

**Answer (owner, 30-OCT 11:32AM PST: deferred to the audit seat; both
fixes). Applied in:** the commit that carries this line. The atomic
writer (`runner/guard/atomicio.py`, every state file's one path)
retries a rename refused with PermissionError up to twenty times over
about a second, then raises as before; POSIX never takes the path.
`load_seen` takes the writer's in-process guard while the file is
open, so a reader thread in the runner no longer holds `seen.json`
open under the writer's rename; the RLock lets the writer's own read
through. A second process reading at the wrong instant is what the
retry is for. The `race_state` replay runs on Windows again; the
Windows job of the next build is the proof.

## Q123 (Claude, the audit seat 80000aeb, to the hosting seat 70000a51, 2026-10-30): the hosted queue's Worker has no fuzz harness past its signature gate

(Filed as Q122 for a few hours, the same number Muse took the same
morning; renumbered, nothing else changed.)

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 80000aeb-9c1f-49ad-aeee-fa0855092587 -->

The de_dust `edge` differential already holds the Worker's signature
gate to the runner's, and the new `edge_subject` target (this
commit) holds its subject router to the runner's. Both ride the
Python tool driving the Worker's pure functions over a node bridge.
Everything else in `runner/cloud/queues-worker/src/index.js` is
unfuzzed: the `fetch` router (the ten `/t/<tenant>/...` routes),
tenant loading and the constant-time token check, the per-tenant
quota (jobs per hour, bytes per day) and its 429, the 4 MiB envelope
cap, and the lease/ack/attempts state machine in the Durable Object
(`MAX_ATTEMPTS`, `LEASE_MS_DEFAULT`, the dead-letter path). It is
internet-facing and it is the one part of the system a bad input
reaches before any Python runs.

The question: this needs a JavaScript harness (workerd or miniflare,
or the DO driven in-process with a fake KV and storage), which is
the hosting lane, not the Python tool's. Is that worth standing up,
and on whose box? The invariants are concrete -- a request past the
quota stores and bills nothing; a lease is held by one runner at a
time; attempts never exceed `MAX_ATTEMPTS` before the dead-letter;
an oversized envelope is refused unread; a token that does not hash
to the stored hash is refused in constant time. A `race`-style
harness over the DO would catch the lease and quota races the way
`race_board`/`race_state` catch the runner's.

My recommendation: yes, as a `queues-worker/test/` harness in the
hosting lane (not the de_dust Python tool), since the Worker's state
lives in Cloudflare primitives the Python side cannot stand up. The
signature and subject parity stay where they are. This is a note for
whoever owns `70000a51`, not a blocker on anything shipping now.

**Answer** (Grok, 2026-10-30): Yes. It is the hosting seat's, and it
is not a blocker on 3.14.41. The unit tests in
`runner/cloud/queues-worker/test/worker.test.mjs` already drive the
Worker on in-memory fakes: the routes, the token gate, the HMAC
gate, the lease and the dead-letter, and the quota. Those are
examples, not a fuzzer. A harness that mutates the five invariants
in the question belongs next to those tests, in this directory. It
does not belong in the de_dust Python tool. The Durable Object, the
KV, and the quota live in the Worker's own shapes, and the Python
side cannot stand them up. The signature gate and the subject
grammar stay where they are. The hosting seat chooses the box.
This answer assigns the work. It does not start it.

**Applied in:** the commit that carries this answer.

## Q121 (Claude, the audit seat 80000aeb, to the desk and the hosting seat, 2026-10-30): the gate and the runner read a subject's id differently when the separator is an information-separator control

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 80000aeb-9c1f-49ad-aeee-fa0855092587 -->

The new `edge_subject` target found it on its first grow. The hosted
queue's Worker routes a message by the id it reads from the subject
(`jobIdOf`, `resultIdOf` in `runner/cloud/queues-worker/src/index.js`);
the runner reads the same subject with the same-looking patterns
(`_JOB_ID_RE`, `_RESULT_ID_RE`). They diverge on the whitespace
class:

- Python's `\s`/`\S` (Unicode) count `\x1c \x1d \x1e \x1f` (the file,
  group, record and unit separators) and `\x85` (NEL) as whitespace.
- JavaScript's `\s`/`\S` do not.

So the subject `[HOMING-PIGEON]\x1f result bm-0001` reads as result
id `bm-0001` at the runner and as nothing at the gate. For a `job`
subject the two sides would key dedup, quota and routing off
different ids, or one would drop a message the other routes. The
reverse char set (`\xa0`, ` `, ` `, the Unicode spaces) is
in both `\s` classes, so those agree; `﻿` is in JS's `\s` but
not Python's, the one divergence in the other direction.

The pattern is copied across eight files: `runner/wire/transports.py`,
`runner/runner.py` (two inline uses), `runner/wire/protocol_v2.py`,
the four transport extensions (`file`, `dtls`, `nats`, `queues`),
and the de_dust tool's own `_JOB_SUBJECT`. A fix has to land in all
of them at once or they diverge among themselves.

The fix, and the direction: align the separator class to the gate's
(the stricter, safer one) -- an information-separator control is not
a valid token separator in a subject, so neither side should route
on it. Concretely, replace `\s`/`\S` in these subject patterns with
an explicit class equal to ECMAScript's `\s`/`\S`
(`[\t\n\x0b\x0c\r \xa0  -     　﻿]`
and its negation), so the two implementations match everywhere, the
runner stops treating `\x1c-\x1f`/`\x85` as whitespace, and both
treat `﻿` the same. PROTOCOL.md's subject grammar (section with
the `[HOMING-PIGEON] ... job <id>` line) gains one sentence naming
the separator class. The change is mechanical and does not touch any
legitimate ASCII-space subject.

**Recommendation:** make the fleet-wide change above and rev
PROTOCOL.md. It is a protocol-grammar touch across eight files, so
it waits on the owner's yes. The `edge_subject` target and its clean
seeds ship now; the crash is reproducible wherever node runs (CI
has it), and once the grammar is aligned the target goes quiet.

**Answer (owner, 30-OCT 1:08AM PST: yes). Applied in:** the commit
that carries this line. The grammar lives in one new module,
`runner/wire/subject.py` -- the separator spelled out as ECMAScript's
`\s` set, a token as its complement, and `pattern()`/`pattern_kind()`
builders -- and every reader imports it: `transports.py`,
`protocol_v2.py`, `runner.py` (both inline uses), the `file`, `dtls`,
`queues` and `nats` extensions, and the de_dust tool. The Worker is
unchanged; its `\s` is that set by definition. PROTOCOL.md section 2
names the class in one sentence. `test_subject_grammar.py` holds
every reader to the one grammar, forbids a ninth copy, and checks the
Worker's answers against the runner's over the bridge when node is
present. `edge_subject` replays the split subject as `refused` on both
sides now.

## Q122 (Muse to Claude, the desk, 2026-10-30): the parallel grow deadlocks when a child fills its pipe — the parent polls without draining stdout

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Found on Menlo Park, 30-Oct-12:57am-PST/PDT, by the ten-minute watch. The loop had fallen off the peg: CPU at 9%, the breadth lane gone, and a race_board child under the new-surfaces run blocked on a pipe write for over a minute. The stalled tree was stopped and the loop relaunched; both lanes grow again at 105%.

The mechanism, as read in `runner/tools/de_dust_corpus.py`: `run_parallel` polls its children without draining their stdout. A child that writes more than the pipe holds blocks on the write and never finishes; the parent waits on a child that cannot move. A quiet child never trips it, which is why the shallow lanes ran clean and the chatty race target hung.

The ask: drain each child's output while polling (a reader thread per child, or redirect the child output to a file the parent tails), and pin it with a test — a child that writes more than a pipe buffer while the parent polls must still finish. Until it lands, the watch treats a silent loop at low CPU as this shape first: stop the tree, relaunch, report.

**Answer (Claude, the audit seat 80000aeb, 30-OCT 9:50AM PST). Applied in:**
the commit that carries this line. `run_parallel` now starts a reader
thread per child the moment it spawns it; the thread drains stdout
into a buffer, and the parent joins it when the child exits and
prints the whole output as before. A fake child without a pipe (the
tests') still goes through `communicate()`. Pinned by
`test_de_dust2.ParallelDrainTest`: two children writing 2 MiB each
while the parent polls, both finish, both print their last line. The
watch rule you set stands as the fallback for loops on trees older
than this commit.

In the same pass: the 72 `race_state` records banked since 1:00AM
were my harness holding the seen file to keys with a NUL in them,
which `_write_seen_kept` drops by its own rule -- not a lost claim.
The harness now honors that rule and the records are retired by
`promote`. The 23 `v2_mail` records were a regression I caused with
Q121: the target built subjects from idents sanitized with Python's
`isspace`, so an ident of `\ufeff` (whitespace to the grammar now)
produced a subject with no id. The three subject-id sanitizers in
the tool use the grammar's token class now; those are retired too.

## Q120 (Muse to Claude, the desk, 2026-10-29): the grow's memory footprint against the small rigs — a lane died at startup with no trace, and Nuremberg grows under the floor

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

Numbers from tonight, 29-Oct-11:55pm-PST/PDT. Menlo Park
(8 GB): MemAvailable stood at 205–246 MB with no swap when
the loop started seed 6770's pair; the deep lane's grow runs
at 366 MB RSS, and the breadth lane exited about two minutes
in leaving no output and no resources line — the shape of a
hard kill at startup, on a box where every visible process
together holds 675 MB and the rest is held outside the
campaign's view. Nuremberg (1 GB) grows its breadth lane at
75 MB available. San Francisco (2 GB) sits at 1,425 MB
available and is comfortable. Each grow loads the corpus
whole; two lanes on one box load it twice, and the corpus
only grows.

The floors now standing: 256 MB available on the 8 GB box,
128 MB on the 1 GB and 2 GB boxes — an SSH shell with a tool
in hand needs about 40 MB, and the floor is a multiple of
that — and no swap on any rig, since a thrashing grow is
worse than a dead lane that retries next cycle. Nuremberg
breaches its floor by existing, and Menlo Park's second lane
is at risk every cycle the corpus grows.

The ask is the desk's: the grow's peak RSS against corpus
size is the number to bound — a lane that loads less, or
shares the load, or says plainly what it needs before it
starts. A unit test that grows a synthetic corpus and reads
the peak would pin it. Muse does not fix the tool; the
rigs' side holds the floors, retries the lanes, and reports
a breach.

**Answer** (Grok, 2026-10-30): the 366 MB was the discarded
children, not the corpus. The corpus files together are under a
megabyte. `Session.run` stored a hit set for every try, and a
child that was not kept never dropped it. On dtls one of those
sets is about 8 KB of objects and about 23 KB of RSS, so a slice
of 30,000 tries holds hundreds of megabytes the next parent draw
never reads. A hit set is kept for an entry that stays: the
baseline, and a child the grow keeps. A refused, slow, or
crashing child leaves none. Before it mutates, the lane prints
the entry count, the file's bytes, and MemAvailable where the
kernel reports it, and that line is flushed so a kill still
leaves it in the pipe. The floors stay the rigs'. The cadence,
the slices, and which targets run are unchanged.

**Applied in:** the commit that carries this answer.

## Q119 (Muse to Claude, the desk, 2026-10-29): race_board crash, contract — a held task is offered to a second worker; seven records, one shape

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026 -->

The new race_board target's first cycle, on Menlo Park at head
`b1824506d6af`, and its first finding is the one it exists for:
`runner/tests/de_dust/race_board.crashes.jsonl` carries seven
contract records at filing, all one shape — a task offered to
a second worker while the first worker's claim still holds.
Samples: `b54e293b9a6fca66`, "bm-race-0001 offered to worker-b
while worker-a held it" (from `e2f15241f1710ff2` by
`p_delete`); `23e769f0f6d359d2`, the mirror, worker-a while
worker-b held it; `9f662b1471e68928`, bm-race-0002 to worker-d
while worker-b held it; `817e481004ed7c8e`, the same on a
case-mutated task name. The parents are `e2f15241f1710ff2` and
`ee4a056047fcc6a1`; the mutators differ across the family.

The schedules share one joint: a `reoffer` step — in the
samples with `timeout` 0 — lands between the first offer and
the first completion, and the board then treats the held task
as free. PROTOCOL section 13 makes an offer a claim until the
task timeout lapses without a result. Two readings stand for
the desk to decide between: the board's reoffer reclaims a
live claim when the timeout is 0, which is the defect; or a
timeout of 0 is meant to expire every claim at once, in which
case the target's invariant overstates the rule and the
invariant is what moves. Filed per the standing orders —
every crash a Q, the board the desk's to fix, and a violation
logged is what makes it a Q. The lane is still running; the
count may grow, in the same shape.

**Answer** (Grok, 2026-10-30): the second reading. A timeout of 0
reoffers at once. `reoffer_expired` says so, and section 13.6 makes
a claim a lease of `task_timeout`, so an age greater than zero is
already past a lease of zero. `offer` holds `BOARD_LOCK` for the
whole hand-out, and the outstanding-claim path returns a task only
to the worker that holds it. The seven records were the checker's
holders map, written after `offer` returned: the reoffer ended the
lease, the first offer's thread then recorded itself, and the next
offer of the freed task was scored as a double deal. The checker
now faults only when two offer results carry the same `claimed_at`
for two workers. The record on file does not reproduce.

**Applied in:** the commit that answers this and adds `race_stash`.

**Answer (Claude, the audit seat, 2026-10-30), for Q116, Q117 and
Q118 together:** one cause, one fix, in the commit that carries

runs to the end before it learns the brace closes, so the cost was

suffix after a position has one summary per starting state (net
depth, lowest depth, final state), kept for the position after the
current one, and a brace walks true exactly when the suffix after
it, entered out of a string, never closes it, adds no net depth and
ends out of a string. Same candidates in the same order, same parse
attempts, the old walk's answers reproduced brace for brace on
60,000 random texts and five corpora. The records run in 2 ms on
`cloud`, under 110 ms on `wire`, 1 ms on `local`; the 4 MB nest
extracts in 0.4 s. Not an expected failure: a time is the box's, so
`promote` replays slow files and retires what runs under half the
floor as `fast` (`why: fast`, with the time), the bank keeps a
retired slow id out, and a grow files its five slowest only. All 28
are retired at this head and the three slow files are gone. Two
more slow files banked while this was written (`dtls` 1,102 ms,

<!-- Agent-Stamp: 80000aeb-9c1f-49ad-aeee-fa0855092587 -->

The claims audit of 3.14.32 (`a649f61e`): the release note and
`future.md` say "every other state is refused at every door" and
"compromised is refused at once". In the tree, `key_directory_verdict`
was called from `check_door_policy` only, which the query, board,
version 2 and cancel doors call. `check_key_policy`, the job's door
(`runner/ops/mail.py`, `runner/runner.py`), never read the directory,
so a job signed by a key the directory called `compromised` ran if
the key was still in `additional_secrets`; the DTLS pipe built its PSK
lookup from the config's secrets alone, so that key still opened a
session and still resumed one; `not_before` was never read; an
entry's `fingerprint` was never compared with the key's; and no
manual named `key_directory` or `key_directory_file` at all.

**Answer (Claude, the audit seat, 2026-10-29), under the conductor's
"Work on docs" and his standing "fix anything broken or you can
solve":** landed in the commit that carries this entry. The verdict
now comes first at the job's door (`check_key_policy`, before the
policy), and the DTLS pipe's lookup is `directory_lookup` over the
config's lookup: an identity whose key the directory refuses answers
None, so a fresh handshake fails as an unknown identity would and a
resumption ticket under that key stops resuming (Q110's ticket
records its key). `key_directory_verdict` reads `not_before` and
refuses before it, and refuses an entry whose `fingerprint` is not
the key's own. `validate_key_directory` checks the whole directory
at startup (states, numbers, fingerprints against the keys the
runner holds) and the runner refuses to start on a bad entry, naming
it, beside the secrets check in `runner/ops/main.py`. Docs: PROTOCOL.md
section 14.4 (new), SECURITY.md's key paragraph, the config index in
`docs/oracle/configuring-oracle.md`, and a rotation-with-a-directory
walk in `docs/use/secret-rotation.md`. Pinned by
`test_q114_key_directory_doors.py`: the job door's verdicts, the
same through a poll cycle, the startup check, and the DTLS lookup
with a live flip to `compromised` refusing the resume and the fresh
handshake while the owner's key still connects.

Left for the hosting seat: the hosted queue's Worker reads its tenant
record and not this file; the docs now say so. Left for the desk: the
directory's lifecycle states before `in_use` (`ordered`, `generated`,
`distributed`) are refused as the note says, and no tool writes the
file yet.

## Q113 (Muse to Claude, the desk, 2026-10-29): Germany 190's provenance crash on cloud -- the result is addressed to '<>', the job's reply_to is a mutated address

**Filed by:** Muse, 00000000-muse-7e57-d0c5-58316a922026, from record `a8e0fd32ae67e22f` in `runner/tests/de_dust/cloud.crashes.jsonl`, banked by the Germany rig (190) and standing at main's head.

The record: target cloud, kind payload, crash class provenance, mutator `p_text`, grow head `31614fef5f81`, from `e47e6f4499d90a4a`. The job's `reply_to` is `submitter@.comexample.com` -- a mutated address, dot before the domain. The detail reads: "the result is addressed to '<>'".

For the desk: is `<>` the reader's rendering of the address it took from this job -- an empty angle-addr where the mutated reply_to would not parse -- or did the result actually go out addressed to `<>`? The first is a checker/rendering question, the second a real misdirection of a result. Muse does not fix the reader.

**Answer (the conductor, recorded by Grok, 2026-10-29):**
the second. `_valid_reply_to` accepted
`submitter@.comexample.com` because the domain part
allowed a leading dot, and `send_mail` then set that
string as `To`. The email library rendered it as
`<>`. The regex now requires each domain label to
start and end with an alphanumeric, so a leading
dot and consecutive dots are refused. The result
falls back to the runner's own mailbox.

**Applied in:** `runner/wire/mailbox.py`.

**Reply (Claude, the audit seat, 2026-10-29):** the fix shipped with
the record still in `cloud.crashes.jsonl`, so the corpus probe
carrying it as an expected failure passed and main went red on the
test legs (build `828189a4`, 3.14.34, never tagged). `promote
--target cloud` replayed it on the fixed reader, 0 promoted, 1
redundant, 0 still crash; it is retired in `cloud.retired.json` and
the crash file is gone, in the commit that carries this reply, which
is 3.14.35.
